answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI, not a separate extension). Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=eastus --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep / ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account with kind = "MongoDB" and appropriate capabilities/settings for Mongo API.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB-style URI for Cosmos Mongo API: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<authDB>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false. Username often includes the account (e.g. user@<account>) and SSL=true (TLS) is required. Port commonly 10255 for TLS endpoints.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Azure Cosmos DB throughput: Request Units per second (RU/s). You choose provisioned RU/s (manual or autoscale) or serverless where available. (No vCore-based tiers in the classic Cosmos DB model.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API you normally authenticate with account keys (primary/secondary keys) or Mongo-style database users (SCRAM credentials). Historically Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication is not supported for the MongoDB API; drivers connect using the Mongo URI with username/password and TLS. (If Entra auth is required for another Cosmos API, that uses RBAC and token flows; not applicable for classic Mongo API.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (for Node.js use the mongodb driver or Mongoose). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB SDK — you use Mongo-compatible drivers against the DocumentDB/Cosmos Mongo endpoint.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: I believe the service exposes vector index types such as HNSW and IVF via provider-specific index options on createIndex, but exact syntax varies. Example (my best guess): db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { name: "embedding_idx", vectorType: "hnsw", metric: "cosine", dims: 1536 }). NOTE: this syntax is vendor-specific and not standard MongoDB; treat as low-confidence.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: For full-text you can use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' })) for basic text search. For richer/hybrid (semantic + vector) search, Azure's recommended approach is to index Cosmos DB data into Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) and perform hybrid queries there; Mongo API doesn't provide Atlas Search-style built-in hybrid search.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Supported protocol versions vary by account configuration; historically Cosmos DB's Mongo API provided compatibility with multiple Mongo versions (3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4, 5.0 in various SKUs). Some Mongo features are missing or emulated: server-side JS execution, certain storage-engine-specific features, and historically limited or no multi-document ACID transactions and limited aggregation stages/behaviour differences. Exact supported wire version must be checked against the account's configured Mongo version.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator for local development (Windows; Docker support limited). Historically the emulator primarily targets the SQL API; MongoDB API support was limited. Best practical approach for Mongo-driver development is to run a local MongoDB server (official mongo Docker image) listening on 27017 for driver-level testing. The Cosmos emulator endpoint and ports differ (SQL endpoints use 8081); Mongo-compatible live testing generally requires a real Cosmos account.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams support on the MongoDB API has been limited historically. Many Cosmos Mongo API versions did not support change streams; if supported it depends on the account's MongoDB wire-version compatibility and may need an account-level feature flag. Assume not available unless the account explicitly advertises change stream support.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (service-specific) for data-plane inspection tools for Cosmos/Mongo-compatible accounts. The general azure MCP server provides broad Azure tooling but the documentdb MCP server contains service-specific inspectors and index/plan viewers for DocumentDB/Cosmos DB.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally named its original NoSQL offering Azure DocumentDB; that service evolved and was rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. The Azure DocumentDB name historically referred to the SQL/Core API of Cosmos. This is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB; Cosmos DB is a Microsoft proprietary, multi-model database with API compatibility layers (SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the MongoDB API Cosmos DB uses Microsoft's Cosmos storage/engine and translates Mongo wire protocol calls to its internal engine. In most cases application code can use Mongo drivers unchanged, but some server-side behaviours, performance characteristics, and unsupported Mongo features (certain aggregation stages, server-side JS, cross-shard transactions, change streams) may require code changes or limitations.

answers.question: Which client library and connection options will this sample use to connect to the DocumentDB cluster from Node.js?
answers.answer: Use Mongoose (npm package 'mongoose') and connect with mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, ssl: true, replicaSet: 'globaldb', authSource: 'admin', retryWrites: false }). Read the full Mongo URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI; do not hard-code credentials. (If the cluster needs extra TLS CA configuration, pass tlsCAFile option.)

answers.question: What index definition does the sample need to efficiently reconstruct a payment timeline?
answers.answer: Create a compound index on paymentReference and timestamp: db.collection.createIndex({ paymentReference: 1, stageTimestamp: 1 }). This supports the aggregation that matches by paymentReference and sorts by stageTimestamp.

answers.question: How will the sample enforce immutability (prevent updates) at the application layer?
answers.answer: Implement Mongoose schema-level guards: set schema pre-hooks for updateOne, updateMany, findOneAndUpdate, replaceOne to throw an error; in pre('save') allow only docs where doc.isNew === true and throw on attempted resave. Optionally expose only an insert API and never call update operations. Example: schema.pre(['updateOne','findOneAndUpdate','updateMany'], function(){ throw new Error('Updates are forbidden; use insert-only audit records'); });

answers.question: What aggregation pipeline will the sample expose to reconstruct the full timeline for a payment reference?
answers.answer: Pipeline: [ { $match: { paymentReference: '<ref>' } }, { $sort: { stageTimestamp: 1 } }, { $group: { _id: '$paymentReference', timeline: { $push: { stage: '$stage', metadata: '$metadata', timestamp: '$stageTimestamp', docId: '$_id' } } } } ]. The API will accept a paymentReference, substitute it into $match, run the pipeline and return the timeline array.

answers.question: What exact DOCUMENTDB_URI format will the sample expect in the environment so it can connect without hard-coded values?
answers.answer: Expect a Mongo-style URI template in DOCUMENTDB_URI, for example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/admin?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false. The sample will pass this URI straight to mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, {...}).
